title: Relationship with cortical error signals

The relationship between basal-ganglia and cortical error signals is best understood not as a duplication of one computation in two anatomical locations, but as a division of labor in signal format and function. Cortical circuits compute high-dimensional, content-rich mismatch signals: errors between predicted and observed sensory input, between higher-level beliefs and lower-level evidence, and, in frontal cortex, between expected and obtained action outcomes. These signals are local to particular layers, columns, cell types, and task variables, and they remain tied to the representational geometry of the cortical world model. Basal-ganglia error signals, by contrast, are comparatively low-bandwidth evaluative signals: dopaminergic activity compresses many details of the current inferred state and recent action history into a teaching quantity that indicates whether the selected trajectory, policy, or outcome was better or worse than expected. Put differently, cortical error signals primarily specify what aspect of the model is wrong, whereas BG error signals primarily specify whether recent state-action sampling should be reinforced, weakened, or revised 1, 2, 3. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Yet the BG error signal does not float free of cortical computation. A central lesson of recent work is that the “expected” term against which dopamine neurons compare outcomes is often cortically constructed. Orbitofrontal cortex contributes the latent task-state information needed to distinguish externally similar situations with different future consequences; when OFC is damaged, dopaminergic error signals lose precisely this model-based structure rather than simply losing a scalar reward expectation 4. Likewise, medial prefrontal cortex shapes dopaminergic prediction errors specifically when the environment contains hidden states that must be inferred, but is much less necessary when the relevant state is fully observable 5. More generally, both theory and experiment now indicate that dopamine errors are computed over belief states rather than over raw sensory surfaces whenever the task demands uncertainty-sensitive inference 6, 7. Even outcome identity learning fits this pattern: value-neutral identity prediction errors in the human midbrain are tied to trial-by-trial updating of outcome-identity expectations in OFC 8. Thus, cortex is not merely a downstream recipient of BG teaching; it provides much of the state-space structure that determines what counts as a dopaminergic error in the first place. The resulting dopaminergic error, however, is not computed over a neutral or unconstrained state space: even when cortex supplies rich latent-state structure, the midbrain channels that evaluate that structure remain strongly biased by interoceptive and homeostatic inputs, so that generalized credit assignment is still anchored to biological preference satisfaction rather than freely ranging over arbitrary cortical discrepancies. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The converse is equally important: dopaminergic/BG error signals do not replace cortical comparators, but rather gate which cortical discrepancies become plasticity-relevant and behaviorally consequential. Cortex can generate its own action-outcome and performance-monitoring errors, particularly in medial frontal territories 2, but these remain distinct from the phasic dopaminergic signal that broadcasts evaluative significance across corticostriatal and mesocortical targets. Mesocortical dopamine operates across multiple temporal and spatial scales, modulating cortical ensembles, oscillatory state, and persistent activity rather than simply delivering a one-shot scalar update to a single synapse 9, 10. Functionally, this makes BG error signaling resemble a projection-specific family of third-factor controllers superimposed on a much richer cortical error field: local cortical circuits compute the detailed mismatch, while dopaminergic channels differentially adjust the gain, persistence, consolidation, and policy relevance of those cortical activity patterns according to both the task-defined inferred state and the organism’s current internal-state weighting.

The resulting architecture is therefore recurrent rather than serial. Cortical error signals help determine the state representations, transition expectations, and task abstractions over which BG evaluative errors are computed; BG error signals, in turn, bias corticostriatal and mesocortical plasticity, action selection, vigor, and gating; the actions thereby selected alter the organism’s future sensory samples and internal states, which then generate the next wave of cortical prediction errors. The cortex and basal ganglia thus participate in a closed-loop error ecology: cortex supplies the structured, high-dimensional content of the discrepancy, whereas the BG supply a compressed, action-oriented evaluation of its behavioral significance. This is why the two classes of signals are neither redundant nor cleanly separable. Cortical error signals can be exquisitely informative yet behaviorally inert unless some subset is selected for policy updating; BG error signals can strongly reinforce or suppress behavior, but only over the state space that cortex and related forebrain structures have rendered legible to them, and only within the viability-constrained objective landscape imposed by the dopaminergic system’s homeostatic/interoceptive grounding.
